record.label: Smooth exclusion-gate calculus
record.statement: For a fixed finite exclusion-gate expression, every transmitted column is centered by parity; receiver, path-ancestor and control-target masks are disjoint as prescribed; controls lie in one commuting algebra and a target may contribute its seed but not its spin. Root maps, adjoints and insertions converge in the weighted topology and obey occupation estimates. Finite local replacements with common parameter expressions, convergent jets and adjoint jets, and uniform polynomial bounds converge inside each fixed surrounding word. A root-mask column has weighted norm at most C√p.
record.boundary: Measurable seed masks are permitted through bounded subsequences with Gaussian almost-everywhere convergence. Grouped finite control coordinates are essential; no dimension-free assertion is made for all flattened color coordinates.

aligned_passages.text:
On a single spin, let $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; $Z_i$ and $X_i$ act on spin $i$
and as the identity on the other spins. Also set
$Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
Then $X|\pm\rangle=\pm|\pm\rangle$ and $Z|+\rangle=|-\rangle$. The cost and mixer are
$$
C_{n,J}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_iZ_j,\qquad B_n=\sum_iX_i.
$$
The two evolutions act differently:
$$
e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}|\sigma\rangle
 =e^{-i\theta H_n(\sigma)}|\sigma\rangle,
\qquad
e^{-i\beta B_n}=\prod_{i=1}^n(\cos\beta\,I-i\sin\beta\,X_i).
$$
The cost evolution changes phases while preserving spin-basis probabilities;
the mixer combines amplitudes of different spin configurations. Cost evolution
alone leaves the initial uniform probabilities unchanged, and a mixer applied
first only multiplies $|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$ by $e^{-in\beta}$.
Alternating them lets the cost-dependent phases change subsequent measurement
probabilities. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022), §2,
equations (1)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).

A depth-$p$ state, with $p$ counting cost–mixer pairs, is
$$
|\psi_{n,p,J}(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)\rangle
=e^{-i\beta_pB_n}e^{-i\gamma_pC_{n,J}}\cdots
 e^{-i\beta_1B_n}e^{-i\gamma_1C_{n,J}}|+\rangle^{\otimes n}.
$$
Here the real angle vectors $\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta$ are
deterministic; $\boldsymbol\gamma$ is separate from the Parisi coefficient
$\gamma(t)$. A *word* means a finite ordered product of cost and mixer
exponentials. Its pattern and angles are fixed independently of $n,J$;
its cost operator depends on $n,J$. Define
$$
v_p(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
 \langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle,
\qquad Q_p=\sup_{\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p}v_p.
$$
The fixed-depth, fixed-angle infinite-size limit is the input from
Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou; it does not contain the later depth
conclusion; see [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).
The source target is $\lim_{p\to\infty}Q_p=P_*$. Its needed lower
bound has the literal quantifiers
$$
\forall\varepsilon>0\quad\exists p\in\mathbb N,
\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p:
\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
\langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle
\ge P_*-\varepsilon.
$$
The same finite list of gates and angles is used for every $n,J$; this is
a limiting expected-energy conclusion. A cost expectation is bounded above by its
maximum eigenvalue, and zero-angle padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing.
It therefore suffices to construct one finite word for every accuracy.
Fixed-instance convergence at increasing depth is a different quantifier
order. Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann's original QAOA argument obtains that
convergence by adiabatic evolution and its Trotter approximation, with depth
allowed to depend on the instance; it does not supply the size-independent
word required here. [Farhi–Goldstone–Gutmann (2014), equation (10) and
§VI, pp. 10–11](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1);
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

The construction first describes local operations on a large tree, where
neighbouring subtrees supply Gaussian inputs. Temporary random labels let
those operations implement the finite classical function of §7. The hard
steps are to implement its aggregations using cost and mixer gates, and
then to replace every use of the labels by ordinary gates while preserving
the energy. Only the resulting ordinary word is transferred to SK.

The choices are nested: fix $\varepsilon$, choose $T<1$, choose a finite
mesh, fix the bounded classical formula and helper probabilities, then
choose the finite gate approximations and remove the seeds. The constants
in a replacement may depend on the surrounding word and on those positive
helper probabilities. [§8.6](#qaoa-assembly-detail) collects the error
allocation before the final $n\to\infty$ limit.
The principal circuit inputs can be read as four local lemmas. Their
proofs remain in the cited manuscript; §§8.2–8.5 reconstruct the
mechanisms and show where each hypothesis enters.

**Smooth replacement.** Fix the height, a finite expression and channel
list, and the required derivatives. Uniform recursive weighted bounds,
convergence of operators and adjoints, and strongly commuting signals with
the stated joint exponential bounds permit substitution inside a fixed
surrounding sequence in the exclusion-gate class defined in §8.2. Constants depend on that fixed family. This is the input
used in §8.3 to replace classical aggregates by finite gates; see
[the foundations, smooth topology and gate calculus][q-gate-calculus].

**Helper contraction and synthesis.** Fix a bounded, finite, type-excluded
odd formula, zero on helpers, and positive helper masses. The contraction
converges smoothly at every cut and for the specified responses. For each
$\eta>0$, finite seeded synthesis gives
$$
\mathcal E(v)\ge\mathcal E(m)-2\eta-2\sqrt{p_H}.
$$
Section 8.4 receives this one fixed seeded word. The source inputs are the
[synthesis statements][q-synthesis-statement] and
[helper theorem][q-helper-statement].

**Seed removal.** Fix that finite seeded word and an energy tolerance.
Reuse the same Gaussian at every occurrence on a vertex. Packet control and
the one-particle comparison then produce one finite ordinary word with the
required energy error. The [seed-removal theorem][q-seed-statement] supplies
an energy conclusion, not merely convergence of seed marginals. It makes the
ordinary-word transfer in §8.5 applicable.

**Fixed-word transfer.** Fix one ordinary word and all its angles before
either size or degree varies. Its positive tree scaled-edge limit equals
its SK expected-energy limit, with the convention conversion in §8.5.
This [fixed-word transfer][q-transfer] closes the thermodynamic-first
theorem in §8.6.

### 8.2 Finite regularisation and the calculus needed for compilation Fix $T,N$ first. The independent continuous rounding coordinate makes the event at the sign discontinuity null. Bounded continuous odd approximations to that sign therefore converge in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. If the bounded output is $m^*$, shrink it to $(1-\kappa)m^*$, with fixed $0<\kappa<1$, before taking $\theta_\kappa=\tfrac12\arcsin((1-\kappa)m^*)$. This margin keeps the derivative of inverse sine bounded on its used range; the output loss is at most $\kappa$ in $L^2$. Then truncate the transmitted functions and approximate the resulting bounded maps by trigonometric polynomials. The source makes these choices from output toward leaves: each outer Lipschitz function is fixed before its inputs are approximated. The Gaussian isometry above converts an error in a transmitted child vector into the same $L^2$ error in its receiving position. Energy continuity then bounds the accumulated loss. The bounded output has the form $m=\sin(2\theta)$; it is the transmitted columns that are bounded, while the Gaussian fields themselves remain unbounded. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, bounded trigonometric approximation][q-bounded-classical]. **The formulas to be synthesized.** A mask is an event in the local seed space invariant under seed reversal. Fix a finite partition into masks, and write $p_R$ for the probability of mask $R$; probabilities used as denominators are positive. For disjoint masks $R,S$, aggregation on the finite regular tree means $$ (A_{RS}f)_i=\mathbf1_R(i)D^{-1/2} \sum_{j\sim i}\mathbf1_S(j)f_j. $$ A formula has a finite expression tree, with bounded measurable functions of the local seed as leaves. Internal operations are such aggregations or pointwise functions of previously formed quantities. Pointwise functions are smooth in their aggregate arguments, with polynomial bounds on all derivatives, uniformly in the seed. Seed dependence itself need not be smooth. Transmitted quantities are odd under simultaneous seed reversal; sent nonlinear functions and output angles are bounded, while aggregate Gaussian fields may be unbounded. An aggregation from $S$ to $R$ excludes $R$ if its transmitted formula uses no vertex of type $R$ below that call. All ancestor exclusions are retained, so a mask cannot recur on one active expression branch. It may recur on a different branch, and distinct branches may share descendants; exclusion asserts no independence between them. Gate targets are likewise excluded from the cross-edge dependencies of their parameters. This makes the physical all-neighbour calculation agree with the intended descendant calculation. For synthesis, reserve disjoint helper masks of positive mass, one per positive aggregation depth, absent from the output dependencies; the bounded odd output angle vanishes on their union. [OpenAI (2026b), Definition 3.3][q-formula-definition]; [Theorem 4.1][q-synthesis-statement]. The types can be encoded together with a Gaussian seed in one raw Gaussian variable: its sign supplies the odd symmetry, while disjoint binary digits of a uniform transform of its absolute value supply independent coordinates. The resulting finite type label is even and the Gaussian seed is odd under reversal. The associated pullback preserves vacuum, parity and $\mathsf L$. Thus adding types preserves the energy identification, rather than assuming an additional circuit resource. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, colours, exclusions and helpers][q-colors]. For the already fixed formula, the exclusion estimate is $$ \|m^{\rm col}-m\|^2\le C(\alpha+p_H), $$ where $\alpha$ is the largest nonhelper type mass and $p_H$ is the total helper mass. Its constant is independent of the number of types. The proof uses orthogonality of the disjoint masks before applying the Lipschitz estimate in the original, fixed list of formula coordinates. Treating the refined types as an arbitrary growing list of independent arguments would not provide this bound. The resulting classical near-optimality proposition supplies a finite bounded odd formula, zero on helpers, with energy as close to $P_*$ as required. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “Type exclusion at small cost” and “Classical near-optimality in synthesis form”][q-colors]. **Which convergence permits the later substitutions?** The gate calculus uses recursive weights $\mathsf W_{h+1}=\mathsf W_0+d\Gamma(\Lambda_h)$, where $\Lambda_h$ is the previous weight restricted to the centred child space. The local weight includes the unbounded raw seed when needed. Its smooth domain is the intersection of all weighted domains. Smooth bounds mean polynomial bounds, with a finite loss of weight powers, for the maps, their adjoints and every specified parameter derivative. The finite height, fixed expression and fixed number of channels matter in these estimates. Strong convergence together with uniform stronger weighted bounds gives convergence in each weaker weighted norm by a spectral cutoff. This is the topology in which one replaces a gate inside a fixed surrounding circuit. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, weights and the topology of convergence][q-weights]. More precisely, the imported smooth-convergence contract is: for each output power $m$ and parameter multi-index $\alpha$, there are an input power $r$, exponent $k$ and constant $C$ such that $$ \|\mathsf W_D^m\partial_x^\alpha F_D(x)\xi\| \le C(1+|x|)^k\|\mathsf W_D^r\xi\|, \qquad \xi\in\bigcap_{q\ge0}\operatorname{Dom}(\mathsf W_D^q). $$ The bound is uniform in degree $D$ and parameter $x$. The same bound and strong convergence on smooth inputs are required for the adjoints and all specified parameter derivatives, with compatible limiting adjoints. Constants may depend on the fixed expression, height, channel list and derivative order. Bounded adjoint derivatives alone do not supply their convergence. At bounded local seeds $\mathsf W_0=1$; for polynomial Gaussian growth the source uses the vacuum-preserving weight $P_0+Q_0(1+|s|)Q_0$, where $P_0$ projects to the local vacuum and $Q_0=1-P_0$. These recursive weights control every generation. They differ from the top-generation number weight in §8.4's packet argument. No uniformity in growing word length, vanishing helper mass or the later seed-removal parameter is implicit in this contract. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth-family bound][q-weights]. One of the essential inputs retains a term beyond the Gaussian field. Let $K_D(x)$ be a smooth unitary family with $K_D(0)=1$, uniformly controlled derivatives and adjoint derivatives that converge smoothly in the stated weighted topology to those of a limiting family $K$, and centred first vacuum derivatives. Write $K_\alpha=\partial_\alpha K(0)=iT_\alpha$ and $K_{\alpha\lambda}=\partial_\alpha\partial_\lambda K(0)$. For a fixed finite parameter list $a$, the source proves $$ K_D(a/\sqrt D)^{\otimes D}\longrightarrow \exp\!\left\{ i\sum_\alpha a_\alpha q(T_\alpha\mathrm{vac}) +\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda}a_\alpha a_\lambda \left\langle K_{\alpha\lambda} +\tfrac12\{T_\alpha,T_\lambda\}\right\rangle_0 \right\}. $$ The second term is imaginary by unitarity. It survives because a second-order change of size $D^{-1}$ occurs in each of $D$ children. Its scalar coefficients become a possibly nonconstant controlled operator when commuting signals replace $a$. For example, $K(x)=e^{ix^2}$ has zero first derivative at zero but $K(a/\sqrt D)^D=e^{ia^2}$ exactly. Keeping only the first derivative would miss even this elementary contribution. The example explains why the term is necessary; the source's weighted product lemma supplies the general convergence and domain bounds. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Products of small unitaries”][q-unitary]. Commuting substitution is justified through a joint spectral calculus and Fourier estimates. It requires the physical control algebra, the self-adjoint signal operators and receiving seed to strongly commute, with joint exponential and weighted derivative bounds as stated in the source. This is stronger than a formal commutator identity on one domain. It does not require a nonsingular covariance matrix or an inverse Gram matrix. Exclusions establish that commuting algebra before a preceding circuit is conjugated through it; conjugation preserves commutation even when the signals share descendants. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Smooth commuting substitution”][q-substitution]. The exact cut recursion records the effect of such shared lower calculations. Let $y$ be the incoming boundary data, $V(y)$ the root matrix, and $m(y)$ its outgoing signals in the current frame. Factoring out the operations wholly inside each child gives $$ E^{[d]}(y)=V(y)\prod_{j\ \mathrm{child}} K_j^{[d-1]}(D^{-1/2}m(y)),\qquad K^{[d]}(y)=u^*E^{[d]}(0)^*E^{[d]}(y)u. $$ Every ratio $K^{[d]}$ equals one at zero. Nevertheless $m(0)$ generally does not vanish, because removing the parent input leaves the root's own signals. The actual zero-boundary root update is $u_{\rm new}=E^{[d]}(0)u$. It is not recovered by setting the entire ratio to one and discarding the baseline operation. Applying the unitary product lemma to this recursion, and then commuting substitution, is the source's smooth gate calculus. Its replacement statement covers a fixed finite surrounding sequence and its required parameter derivatives; it does not assert uniformity for arbitrary sequences whose length or channel count grows. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth gate calculus and its cut recursion][q-gate-calculus].
